```{r m4-setup, include=FALSE}
have_gmp <- requireNamespace("gmp", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = have_gmp, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  out.width = "100%")
options(width = 82)
```

In `postrank`, two entities can "tie" in two completely different senses:

1. **A shared grade in the report (`g_i = g_j`)** is a reporting action. It
   leaves the pair unordered—withholding an ordering claim—without saying that
   the two entities have equal target values.
2. **Exact equality in the posterior (`theta_i = theta_j`)** is an event under
   your posterior distribution before any grades are chosen.

Those two concepts need not coincide: two entities with unequal targets often
receive the same grade when \(\tau\) makes ordering them too risky, and a
discrete or structural posterior can assign positive probability to
\(\theta_i = \theta_j\) before grading begins. This article explains that
distinction, defines the **equality-neutral loss** used in **tie-aware mode**
(`postrank_tie_*`), and walks through exact finite-law examples without model
fitting or an optimization solver. Building and evaluating exact finite-law
inputs requires the suggested `gmp` package (`install.packages("gmp")`).

```{r m4-dependency-note, echo=FALSE, results='asis', eval=TRUE}
if (!have_gmp) cat("**Computation skipped:** the suggested package `gmp` is not installed. Install `gmp` and rebuild to run the exact finite-law examples.\n")
```

## Exact target equality versus a shared grade {#a-tie-in-the-target-is-different-from-a-tie-in-the-report}

**Exact target equality** (\(\theta_A = \theta_B\)) is a property of the joint
posterior distribution. It has probability zero under standard continuous
posteriors for distinct entities, probability between zero and one under
discrete posteriors or spike-and-slab / clustering models, and probability one
when two entities share the exact same structural parameter.

**A shared grade** (\(g_A = g_B\)) is a reporting choice: `postrank` leaves `A`
and `B` unordered; it does not say the entities are equal. Equal
posterior means do not imply \(\Pr(\theta_A = \theta_B) > 0\), and rounding
continuous MCMC draws creates artificial ties rather than genuine posterior
equality. Conversely, continuous marginal distributions alone do not rule out
exact ties if two entities share the same latent variable in the joint model.
(Rules that treat small nonzero differences \(|\theta_A - \theta_B| \le \delta\)
as practically equivalent define a separate margin-based decision problem;
`postrank` uses exact equality with zero margin.) See Lee (2026), Chapter 9,
[Different meanings of a tie](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/09-targets-actions-laws.html#different-meanings-of-a-tie).

## Weak-error loss versus equality-neutral loss {#two-losses-make-different-choices-at-equality}

Orient targets so that larger values receive higher priority toward Grade 1.
Standard `postrank` functions use **weak-error loss** on tie-free inputs:
reporting `A` ahead of `B` counts an error whenever \(\theta_A \le \theta_B\),
and leaving the pair unordered costs \(\tau\) in every state.

For posteriors in which \(\Pr(\theta_A = \theta_B) > 0\), `postrank`'s separate
**tie-aware mode** (`postrank_tie_*`) uses **equality-neutral loss**:

- Only strict reversals (\(\theta_A < \theta_B\) when `A` is reported ahead of
  `B`) count as wrong-direction errors (`cost = 1`).
- Leaving a pair unordered costs \(\tau\) only when \(\theta_A \ne \theta_B\).
- When \(\theta_A = \theta_B\), **exact equality has zero loss whether the pair
  is ordered in either direction or left unordered**:

| Posterior state | Weak loss: `A` ahead of `B` | Weak loss: unordered | Equality-neutral: `A` ahead of `B` | Equality-neutral: unordered |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| \(\theta_A > \theta_B\) | `0` | \(\tau\) | `0` | \(\tau\) |
| \(\theta_A = \theta_B\) | `1` | \(\tau\) | `0` | `0` |
| \(\theta_A < \theta_B\) | `1` | \(\tau\) | `1` | \(\tau\) |

Equality-neutral loss also assigns cost `0` to reporting `B` ahead of `A` when
\(\theta_A = \theta_B\). Thus zero equality-neutral loss means zero strict
reversals and zero withheld distinct pairs—not that every ordered pair is
strictly unequal. Standard `postrank()` inputs reject positive tie probability
rather than silently switching losses; to use equality-neutral loss, build
inputs explicitly with `as_postrank_tie_draws()` and `postrank_tie_pairwise()`.
See Lee (2026), Chapter 11,
[An equality-neutral extension of directional loss](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/11-multicriteria-loss.html#sec-tie-aware-loss).

## A finite two-entity posterior with exact ties {#specify-a-complete-two-entity-law}

Consider two fictional entities `A` and `B` on one criterion (`score`), where
`B` equals `1` in every state and `A` takes values `0`, `1`, and `2` with
probabilities `0.1`, `0.4`, and `0.5`:

```{r m4-law}
library(postrank)

states <- lapply(c(0, 1, 2), function(a)
  matrix(c(a, 1), nrow = 2,
    dimnames = list(entity = c("A", "B"), criterion = "score")))
masses <- c(1L, 4L, 5L)
law_table <- data.frame(A = c(0, 1, 2), B = 1,
  Probability = masses / sum(masses))
knitr::kable(law_table)
```

An exact finite-law input in tie-aware mode (identified by input-format version
`schema_version = "tie-aware-input-0.1"` and `input_kind = "exact_finite_posterior"`)
requires the suggested `gmp` package (`install.packages("gmp")`) to verify
integer target states and positive integer probability numerators sharing a
common denominator, and retains exact rational probabilities alongside the
double-precision arrays in `postrank_tie_pairwise()`. You also record where the
input came from (`provenance`: the script or program `producer`, an `artifact_id`,
and its SHA-256 `artifact_hash`) and set `not_empirical_posterior_relabeling = TRUE`
to confirm that the listed states define a true discrete distribution rather
than relabeled Monte Carlo draws. We split this setup into three short helpers:

```{r m4-targets-context}
tie_targets_context <- function(criteria, description) {
  list(
    targets = lapply(criteria, function(k) list(
      criterion_id = k, estimand = paste("Specified", k, "target"),
      entity_population = "Fictional entities in the displayed law",
      time_reference = "Mathematical example", units = "Score units",
      source_transform = "Identity",
      identification_basis = "Defined by the listed states",
      orientation = "higher_priority")),
    context = list(cohort_id = "m4-example", data_version = "1",
      data_conditioning = "Stipulated finite distribution",
      model_summary = description)
  )
}
```

```{r m4-tie-declarations}
tie_declarations <- function(criteria, description) {
  c(tie_targets_context(criteria, description), list(
    identification = list(status = "identified_declared",
      note = "Targets are defined directly by the listed states"),
    tie_policy = list(rule = "equality_neutral", declared = TRUE,
      justification = "Equal values in a state represent exact target equality",
      observed_tie_action = "accept_declared_exact_equality"),
    equality = list(basis = "exact_finite_law",
      justification = "Equality checked across all positive-mass states",
      criterion_classes = NULL)
  ))
}
```

```{r m4-finite-law}
finite_input <- function(states, masses, description) {
  ids <- rownames(states[[1]]); criteria <- colnames(states[[1]])
  decl <- tie_declarations(criteria, description)
  as_postrank_tie_draws(c(list(
    schema_version = "tie-aware-input-0.1", input_kind = "exact_finite_posterior",
    dependence_mode = "joint_model", requested_functional = "expected_rank_loss",
    entity_ids = ids, criterion_ids = criteria,
    provenance = list(producer = "m4-ties-and-withholding", artifact_id = "law",
      artifact_hash = digest::digest(list(states, masses), algo = "sha256"),
      construction_note = "Exact finite distribution",
      created_at = format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC", format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")),
    finite_law = list(denominator = sum(masses), value_representation = "safe_integer",
      states = lapply(seq_along(states), function(s) list(
        state_id = paste0("state-", s), mass_numerator = masses[s], theta = states[[s]])),
      law_definition = description, not_empirical_posterior_relabeling = TRUE)
  ), decl))
}
```

Passing those three states to `postrank_tie_pairwise()` decomposes the pair
`(A, B)` into three probability arrays:

```{r m4-probabilities}
input <- finite_input(states, masses,
  "B equals 1; A is 0, 1, or 2 with probabilities 1/10, 4/10, 5/10")
pw <- postrank_tie_pairwise(input)
probabilities <- data.frame(
  Event = c("A < B (strict error of A ahead of B)", "A = B (equality)",
    "A != B (distinctness)", "B < A (strict error of B ahead of A)"),
  Probability = c(pw[["b"]]["A", "B", "score"], pw[["t"]]["A", "B", "score"],
    pw[["d"]]["A", "B", "score"], pw[["b"]]["B", "A", "score"])
)
knitr::kable(probabilities)
```

For distinct entities `i` and `j` on criterion `k`:

- `b[i, j, k]` is the **strict directional-error probability**
  \(\Pr(\theta_{ik} < \theta_{jk})\) when `i` is graded ahead of `j`.
- `t[i, j, k]` is the **equality probability** \(\Pr(\theta_{ik} = \theta_{jk})\).
- `d[i, j, k]` is the **distinctness probability**
  \(\Pr(\theta_{ik} \ne \theta_{jk}) = 1 - t_{ij,k}\).

Off-diagonal entries satisfy `b[i, j, k] + b[j, i, k] = d[i, j, k]`, which is
below `1` whenever `t[i, j, k] > 0` (here `0.1 + 0.5 = 0.6`). Using `1 - 0.1`
for the reverse strict error would mistakenly add the `0.4` equality mass.
Diagonal entries are `NA`.

## Evaluating the three two-entity gradings {#evaluate-directions-and-withholding}

With two entities there are three possible gradings: `A` ahead of `B` (`1/2`),
`B` ahead of `A` (`2/1`), and leaving the pair unordered (`1/1`). At
`tau = 0.25`, `postrank_tie_evaluate()` scores each grading under
equality-neutral loss:

```{r m4-actions}
tau <- 0.25
actions <- list(
  `A ahead of B` = c(A = 1L, B = 2L),
  `B ahead of A` = c(A = 2L, B = 1L),
  Unordered = c(A = 1L, B = 1L)
)
evaluations <- lapply(actions, postrank_tie_evaluate,
  pairwise = pw, weights = c(score = 1), tau = tau)
p <- masses / sum(masses)
weak_risk <- c(sum(p * (law_table[["A"]] <= law_table[["B"]])),
  sum(p * (law_table[["B"]] <= law_table[["A"]])), tau)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Action = names(actions), Weak_loss = weak_risk,
  Equality_neutral_loss = vapply(evaluations, `[[`, numeric(1), "primary_risk")
), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

Under equality-neutral loss, reporting `A` ahead of `B` has loss `0.100`,
beating `1/1` (`0.25 * 0.6 = 0.150`). Under weak-error loss, the `0.4` equality
probability is counted as a wrong direction (`0.1 + 0.4 = 0.500`), so weak loss
leaves the pair unordered (`0.250`).

For \(n\) entities and \(K\) criteria with weights \(w_k\) summing to `1`, let
\(E_k(g)\) sum `b[i, j, k]` over ordered pairs \(g_i < g_j\), \(D_k(g)\) sum
`d[i, j, k]` over ordered pairs, and \(T_k\) sum `d[i, j, k]` over **all**
\(M = \binom{n}{2}\) unordered pairs. Writing \(E_w = \sum_k w_k E_k\),
\(D = \sum_k w_k D_k\), and \(T = \sum_k w_k T_k\), the equality-neutral loss is

\[
R(g) = \frac{E_w(g) + \tau\{T - D(g)\}}{M}
     = R_0 + \frac{E_w(g) - \tau \, D(g)}{M},
\qquad R_0 = \frac{\tau \, T}{M}.
\]

Thus the **all-withheld risk** `R0` (`0.150` here) is below \(\tau\) whenever
any pair has positive equality probability on a positive-weight criterion, and
the centered objective `raw_Z` subtracts `tau * D` rather than `tau * N`:

```{r m4-risk-identity}
forward <- evaluations[["A ahead of B"]]
c(
  direct = forward[["primary_risk"]],
  baseline_plus_centered = forward[["R0"]] + forward[["raw_Z"]] / forward[["M"]],
  all_withheld = evaluations[["Unordered"]][["primary_risk"]]
)
```

## Raw-pair versus distinct-pair denominators {#read-the-denominator-as-carefully-as-the-numerator}

In tie-aware mode, `N / M` is the fraction of all pairs placed in different
grades, whereas `D / T` (`D_over_T`) is the fraction of weighted distinct-pair
mass that is ordered. Similarly, `E_over_N` divides expected strict errors
\(E_k\) by `N`, whereas `E_over_D` divides \(E_k\) by criterion \(k\)'s ordered
distinctness sum \(D_k\):

```{r m4-denominators}
denominators <- do.call(rbind, lapply(evaluations, function(x)
  data.frame(N = x[["N"]], D = x[["D"]], T = x[["T"]],
    `E/N` = unname(x[["E_over_N"]]), `E/D` = unname(x[["E_over_D"]]),
    `D/T` = x[["D_over_T"]], check.names = FALSE)))
knitr::kable(denominators, digits = 3)
```

For `A ahead of B`, `0.1` expected strict errors per ordered pair (`E/N = 0.100`)
corresponds to `0.1 / 0.6 = 0.167` (`1/6`) expected strict errors per distinct
comparison (`E/D`). Both are ratios of posterior expectations (`E[errors] / E[distinct]`),
not expectations of draw-by-draw ratios.

When `A` and `B` are equal with probability `1` and left unordered, all three
denominators `N`, `D`, and `T` are `0`, so `E_over_N`, `E_over_D`, and
`D_over_T` are `NA` and `R0 = 0`:

```{r m4-zero-denominators}
equal_pw <- postrank_tie_pairwise(finite_input(states[2], 1L,
  "A and B both equal 1 with probability 1"))
equal_hold <- postrank_tie_evaluate(actions[["Unordered"]], equal_pw,
  weights = c(score = 1), tau = tau)
equal_hold[c("N", "D", "T", "E_over_N", "E_over_D", "D_over_T", "R0")]
```

## Agreement when tie probability is zero {#check-the-zero-tie-case}

If we move the `0.4` tie mass onto `(A = 2, B = 1)`—giving probabilities `0.1`
and `0.9` with zero tie probability—then `d = 1`, `D = N`, `T = M`, and
`R0 = tau`, so `postrank_tie_evaluate()` and standard `postrank_evaluate()` give
identical losses for every grading:

```{r m4-no-ties}
no_tie <- postrank_tie_pairwise(finite_input(states[c(1, 3)], c(1L, 9L),
  "A is 0 or 2 with probabilities 1/10 and 9/10; B equals 1"))
ordinary <- postrank_probabilities(
  no_tie[["b"]], event = "directional_error", zero_ties = TRUE, margin = 0,
  source = list(kind = "analytic_reference",
    description = "Two-state probabilities without ties",
    conditioning = "Stipulated two-state distribution"),
  targets = c(score = "Higher score means higher priority")
)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Action = names(actions),
  Standard_loss = vapply(actions, function(g)
    postrank_evaluate(g, ordinary, c(score = 1), tau)[["primary_risk"]], numeric(1)),
  Equality_neutral_loss = vapply(actions, function(g)
    postrank_tie_evaluate(g, no_tie, c(score = 1), tau)[["primary_risk"]], numeric(1))
), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

Whenever every positive-weight criterion has zero equality probability, the two
objectives coincide across all gradings (zero-weight criteria do not change the
loss).

## Active-profile equality constraint {#keep-identical-active-profiles-in-the-same-grade}

Without an extra safeguard, two entities that are equal with probability `1` on
every active criterion (`D = 0`) could be placed in different grades at zero
equality-neutral cost! Tie-aware mode prevents such arbitrary splits through the
**active-profile equality constraint**: if two entities share the same
criterion equality class on **every positive-weight criterion** (equal across
all states of an exact finite law, or declared in the same structural class in
`equality$criterion_classes` on Monte Carlo draws), they belong to the same
**active-profile equality class** and must receive the same grade in any
solution returned by `postrank_tie_solve()`.

Consider a single-state three-entity example with a `shared` criterion and an
`individual` criterion:

```{r m4-guard-state}
profile_state <- matrix(c(2, 2, 0, 0, 1, 2), nrow = 3,
  dimnames = list(entity = c("A", "B", "C"),
    criterion = c("shared", "individual")))
knitr::kable(profile_state)
```

```{r m4-guard-eval}
profile_pw <- postrank_tie_pairwise(finite_input(list(profile_state), 1L,
  "Single state with shared and individual criteria"))
split_grade <- c(A = 1L, B = 2L, C = 3L)
only_shared <- postrank_tie_evaluate(split_grade, profile_pw,
  c(shared = 1, individual = 0), tau)
both_active <- postrank_tie_evaluate(split_grade, profile_pw,
  c(shared = 0.5, individual = 0.5), tau)
data.frame(Weights = c("1 / 0", "0.5 / 0.5"),
  Guard_satisfied = c(only_shared[["guard_satisfied"]], both_active[["guard_satisfied"]]))
```

When only `shared` has positive weight (`1 / 0`), `A` and `B` are identical on
all active criteria, so `split_grade` violates the constraint
(`guard_satisfied = FALSE`). When both criteria have positive weight (`0.5 / 0.5`),
their distinct `individual` values separate them (`guard_satisfied = TRUE`).
`postrank_tie_evaluate()` still computes the loss of a constraint-violating
grading so you can inspect it, whereas `postrank_tie_problem()` enforces the
constraint while keeping all original entities and \(M = 3\) pair counts intact:

```{r m4-problem}
problem <- postrank_tie_problem(profile_pw,
  weights = c(shared = 1, individual = 0), tau = tau, G_max = 3L)
problem[["guard"]][["classes"]]
problem[["M"]]
```

Notice that `M` stays `3` (`A` and `B` are constrained to share a grade, not
merged into a single unweighted entity). Over the unrestricted weighted
at-most-`G_max` family, at least one global minimizer always satisfies the
active-profile equality constraint; see Lee (2026), Chapter 11,
[Same-grade guard for identical active profiles](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/11-multicriteria-loss.html#a-guard-for-identical-active-profiles).

For Monte Carlo draw inputs (`as_postrank_tie_draws()`), **criterion equality
partitions** (`equality$criterion_classes[[k]]`) must be declared from structural
knowledge of the model and verified against the draws—accidental ties in a
finite sample or ties created by rounding continuous draws do not define
structural equality classes.

## Scope of tie-aware mode {#use-the-supported-mode-deliberately}

Tie-aware mode (`postrank_tie_*`, inspected via `postrank_tie_capabilities()`)
supports exact finite distributions and joint equal-weight IID or MCMC draw
inputs, weighted expected-loss problems with `G_max` and the active-profile
equality constraint, and direct mixed-integer solving via `strategy = "label_mip"`
using HiGHS or licensed Gurobi. Solving requires installing `highs`
(`install.packages("highs")`) or Gurobi, so the solver call below is shown
without running here:

```{r m4-optional-solve, eval=FALSE}
fit <- postrank_tie_solve(
  problem, backend = "highs",
  control = postrank_control(strategy = "label_mip", time_limit = 30,
    threads = 1L, seed = 1304L)
)
```

Per-criterion error budgets `q`, `objective = "minimax"`, `exact_G`,
`strategy = "staged"`, separate criterion draw matrices, normal/mixture
coefficients, and `postrank_probabilities()` inputs are not available in
tie-aware mode. Tie-aware fits provide `print()`,
`format()`, and `summary()` methods with results in `fit$grade`,
`fit$evaluation`, and `fit$objective`; standard common-grade accessors
(`get_grades()`, `get_risk()`, `get_profile()`), baselines, HTML reports,
`postrank_plot_*()` figures, Monte Carlo diagnostics, and IID bounds do not
accept tie-aware objects.

For full derivations and capability details, see JoonHo Lee (2026), *Decisions
from Noisy Multidimensional Indicators: Theory, Evidence, and Posterior Grading*
(`citation("postrank")`): Chapter 9 (`#different-meanings-of-a-tie`), Chapter 11
(`#sec-tie-aware-loss` and `#a-guard-for-identical-active-profiles`), and
Appendix D,
[Equality-neutral implementation and capability limits](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/appendices/D-package-correspondence.html#sec-package-tie-aware).
See also
[Posterior ranking, integer grades, and reporting loss](m1-ranking-and-loss.html),
[Posterior representations and pairwise comparison probabilities](m3-posterior-inputs.html),
and
[Computing grades, choosing settings, and reading solver bounds](m5-computing-grades.html).
